title: A discount is still a price.
dek: Same jacket, €200 crossed out and €120 in red: the brain counts €80 won. 98% of the Black Friday deals one study followed were the same price or cheaper on another day of the year.
whyThisIdea: Toate ideile rămase în backlog sunt marcate ca prea apropiate de articole publicate, așa că am adăugat una nouă, legată de săptămâna asta: vinerea viitoare (27 noiembrie) e Black Friday. Anchoring are cifre verificabile (Tversky & Kahneman 1974, Ariely și colegii 2003, studiul Which? din 2021) și se leagă de „Enough is a number you pick.”, dar unghiul e nou: prețul tăiat, nu stilul de viață.

entry.title: A discount is still a price.
entry.titleHtml: A discount is still a price.
entry.dek: Same jacket, €200 crossed out and €120 in red: the brain counts €80 won. 98% of the Black Friday deals one study followed were the same price or cheaper on another day of the year.
body: Have you ever asked yourself why a price with a line through it feels so much better than a price without one? Next Friday, the 27th of November, is Black Friday, and the emails have already started - most of them with some version of “up to 70% off” in the subject. And if you are a student like me, with a small budget and a long list of things you “kind of need”, this is probably the most dangerous week of the year. So the question is: when a shop shows you two prices, which one are you actually looking at? Let’s start from the beginning.

The thing I want to look at is the discount itself - the old price crossed out, and the new one next to it in red. I met it the way everybody does, on my phone, between two notifications. To make it simple, let’s take one example and keep it for the whole article: a jacket that was €200 and is now €120. Forty percent off. It is a very good feeling, and that feeling is exactly what made me suspicious.

Firstly, let’s split the title in two, the way I like to do. “A discount” and “a price”. The discount is the number they want you to look at: €80, or 40%. The price is the number that actually leaves your account: €120. In the shop they sit next to each other, the big red one and the small black one, and the brain does a funny thing - it counts the €80 as money you won. But those €80 only exist if you were going to buy that jacket anyway, at €200. If you were not, nothing was saved. You just spent €120 on a jacket you did not plan to buy. <u>A discount saves you money only on things you were already going to buy.</u> For everything else, it is not a saving, it is a reason.

Secondly, why does the crossed-out number work so well, even when we know it is there to sell us something? The name for it is anchoring. In 1974, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman did an experiment that sounds almost like a joke. People watched a wheel of fortune that was set to stop on 10 or on 65. Then they were asked if the percentage of African countries in the United Nations was higher or lower than that number, and after that, to guess the real percentage. The people who saw 10 gave a median answer of 25%. The people who saw 65 gave a median answer of 45%. A number that everybody in the room knew was random moved the answer by 20 points.

And it works with money too. In 2003, Dan Ariely, George Loewenstein and Drazen Prelec published a paper with a very strange title: “Coherent Arbitrariness”. They asked students to write down the last two digits of their social security number, to say if they would pay that many dollars for everyday products (a bottle of wine, for example), and then to say how much they would really pay. The number had nothing to do with the wine. But the students with the higher numbers said values that were from 57% to 107% higher than the students with the lower ones. The crossed-out €200 is the same kind of number. It is not there to inform you. It is there to be the first number you see.

Now let’s do the arithmetic, because Black Friday has one more trick. Very often the jacket is already 40% off and then there is an “extra 20% off sale prices” on top. 40 plus 20 sounds like 60%. Let’s check it:
€200 × 0.60 = €120
€120 × 0.80 = €96
€96 out of €200 means you pay 48%, so the real discount is 52%, not 60%. At 60% the jacket would have been €80, so the label in your head is €16 nicer than the receipt. It is not a lie, the 20% is real - it is just 20% of a smaller number. And the €96 is still €96 that leaves your account, whatever the red number says.

Thirdly, and this is the part that surprised me the most. In 2021, the British consumer organisation Which? followed 213 products that were on offer on Black Friday and checked their prices in the six months before and the six months after. 208 of them, which is 98%, were the same price or cheaper at some other moment of the year. So it is not only the old price that is an anchor - the day itself is one. “Black Friday” makes you feel that the price is low because of the date, not because of the price. But I have to be fair here too: that was one study, in one country, on the products they chose. It does not mean that there are no real discounts. If you were going to buy a laptop anyway, and on Friday it is really cheaper than usual, buying it on Friday is just smart.

So here is what I am going to do, because an article like this is worthless if it ends only in agreement. Before Friday, before I open a single email, I write down the things I actually need, and next to each one, the price I would normally pay for it. On Friday, I only look at that list. And for anything that is not on it, I ask myself one question: would I buy this at the price at the bottom, if there was no other price above it? If the answer is no, the discount was the thing I wanted, not the product.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I really believe that most of what we “save” on Black Friday is money we spent, and that the crossed-out price is the most effective number in the whole shop. But I have to be honest about two things. The old price is not always useless - if you know how much something usually costs, it is real information, and waiting for a sale on a thing you need is a real saving, not a trick. And my list will probably make me miss a good deal or two this year. I am okay with that. What I take from it is smaller than “never buy on sales”: <u>look at the price you pay, not at the price you did not.</u>
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
